docs.title: Switched Control for Quantized Feedback Systems: Invariance and Limit Cycle Analysis
docs.citation: Papadopoulos A.V., Terraneo F., Leva A., Prandini M. (2018). IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control 63(11):3775-3786. doi:10.1109/TAC.2018.2797246. arXiv:1701.07482 (v2 2017-06-12)
docs.why: Integrator with a one-step delay whose input and output are both quantized, the same shape as our measure, round, move loop with 0.01/0.05 command steps. Gives the necessary and sufficient conditions for a limit cycle under a constant disturbance (backlash-like bias) and a switched controller that holds the output at zero or one step. Only the abstract was checked.

docs.title: A General Harmonic Rule Controller for Run-to-Run Process Control
docs.citation: He F., Wang K., Jiang W. (2009). IEEE Transactions on Semiconductor Manufacturing 22(2):232-244. doi:10.1109/tsm.2009.2017627
docs.why: Generalizes the 1/k harmonic rule (Grubbs) for removing an initial setup bias. Shows it is more robust than EWMA when the process gain is estimated with error. This answers full versus partial moves, gain-mismatch robustness, and how to combine measurements across turns. The author-hosted PDF was downloaded and page 1 checked.

docs.title: A Bivariate Dead Band Process Adjustment Policy
docs.citation: del Castillo E., Göb R. (2019). arXiv:1912.08337 [stat.ME]. No journal version was confirmed.
docs.why: Trades a fixed cost per adjustment (for us, one turn) against a quadratic off-target loss for two responses and two controllable factors. The optimal policy is a 2D dead band, with analytic loss and average adjustment interval. This applies directly to the Y,T joint stop rule and to sizing the dead band. Only the abstract was checked.

docs.title: Stability analysis of semiconductor manufacturing process with EWMA run-to-run controllers
docs.citation: Ai B., Wong D.S.-H., Jang S.-S. (2015). arXiv:1510.08946. No journal version was confirmed.
docs.why: Derives the stability region of the EWMA gain under model-gain mismatch and metrology delay, using Routh-Hurwitz and Lyapunov methods. This bounds how far the move gain can be reduced or raised before overshoot or divergence. Only the abstract was checked.

docs.title: Robot system using visual feedback
docs.citation: US 9,517,563 B2, FANUC Corporation (inventor Keisuke Watanabe). Filed 2015-02-10, granted 2016-12-13, priority JP 2014-025600.
docs.why: The loop is capture, compute the robot move, then judge arrival when the computed move is below a threshold (e.g. 0.5 mm, or 1 pixel of feature difference). Otherwise the robot moves and the image is retaken. This is an industrial example of a dead-band stop rule on the computed move. The USPTO PDF was checked by OCR.

docs.title: Step-and-repeat alignment and exposure method and apparatus
docs.citation: US 4,910,679 A, Canon K.K. (Takahashi K., Kosugi M.). Filed 1989-04-13, granted 1990-03-20, priority JP 60-058535 / 60-090891.
docs.why: Updates the stored correction as Q = (1-R)Q + R*C, which becomes the running average (harmonic rule) when R = 1/P. States that the same learning applies to the X, Y and theta errors. This is patent evidence for partial (weighted) correction under measurement noise. The USPTO PDF was checked by OCR.

docs.title: Image stabilization apparatus and control method thereof, and storage medium
docs.citation: US 9,635,266 B2, Canon K.K. (inventor Masaaki Noguchi). Filed 2015-04-17, granted 2017-04-25, priority JP 2014-087589.
docs.why: Puts an upper limit (Δshiftmax) on the correction change per update and carries the excess to later updates as a 'correction remaining amount'. The field is image stabilization, not robotics, but it states the max-move-per-step and carry-over rule explicitly. The USPTO PDF was checked by OCR.

existing.why: Q1, Q6. Discrete look-and-move gives e(k+1) = (I - g J^-1 J) e(k). The gain and the Jacobian estimation error together set convergence and overshoot. The eigenvalue (0,2) condition limits the gain.
Q1, Q4. Our structure is a static look-and-move. Its own summary says the remaining issues are loop gain, sensitivity error and quantization.
Q6. Stability conditions under different interaction-matrix estimates.
Q6. Convergence problems when the calibration or model error is large.
Q5. Propagation of measurement error into the final positioning error. This informs the dead-band width relative to noise.
Q6, Q7. Online Jacobian (gain) update from executed moves and image change, as a remedy for gain mismatch.
Q6, Q7. Dynamic quasi-Newton Jacobian estimation in uncalibrated visual servoing.

Q2, Q5, Q8. Stops when the error is at or below the allowable value, skips correction when the measurement is unusable, and approaches from one side without passing the target, which avoids reversal and backlash.
Q8. Target-position correction that depends on the backlash direction.
Q8. Diagnosis of lost motion, which sets the backlash size that the final-approach rule must handle.
Q5, Q7. Repeated teaching until within an allowable range, with variance-based updating of the correction.
Q4, Q8. Survey of backlash in control loops, including limit cycles and compensation.
Q8. Gear backlash identification and compensation.
Q7, Q8. Iterative learning compensation of hysteresis using vision measurement across iterations.
Q1, Q9. Look-and-move stage alignment repeated until the error is below a criterion (3 um, about 480 ms).
Q1, Q9. XXY stage visual servo alignment of linear and angle axes with error analysis.
Q9. Decoupled control of rotation and translation, which informs moving Y and T together or in sequence.
